dataset.source: TravisTorrent travistorrent_5_3_2016 (Figshare 10.6084/m9.figshare.19314170, CC BY 4.0; Beller, Gousios & Zaidman, MSR 2017)

population.label_rule: label 1 = failed or errored, 0 = passed; canceled/started excluded

findings.title: Failure rate by change size
findings.question: Do builds with more changed lines (source + test) fail more often?

population.description: labelled builds; total churn = src_churn + test_churn lines

findings.summary: Failure rate is 28.09% (95% CI 27.80–28.38%, n=94,546) for 0–100 changed lines and 36.31% (33.45–39.28%, n=1,041) for >5,000 lines: a difference of +8.22 pp (95% CI +5.34 to +11.20 pp), risk ratio 1.29 (95% CI 1.19–1.40). Rates rise monotonically across the 5 buckets. Pearson χ² = 224.2 (dof 4, n=128,617), p = 2.29e-47; effect size Cramér's V = 0.042 (negligible).
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. Large changes may concentrate in particular projects, periods or change types (merges, refactors, dependency updates).
With n in the tens of thousands even negligible differences reach tiny p-values: read the effect size and its interval, not the p-value.
Churn counts lines in source and test files only (TravisTorrent definitions, docs/data/FEATURE_DEFINITIONS.md); documentation and other files add no lines.

findings.title: Source churn vs test churn vs failure
findings.question: How do source-change size and test changes relate to failure, jointly?

population.description: labelled builds; quartiles of src_churn; tests changed = test_churn > 0; test-change ratio = test_churn / (src_churn + test_churn)

tests_changed_within_projects.description: tests changed vs not, stratified by project

findings.summary: Source-churn quartile cut points (labelled builds, linear interpolation): 0 / 10 / 77 lines. Builds that change tests (test churn > 0) fail at 31.46% vs 28.02% without (+3.43 pp, 95% CI +2.88 to +3.99 pp). Within source-churn quartiles the tests-changed minus no-test-change difference is: Q1 +6.57 pp (+5.37 to +7.79 pp); Q2 +2.01 pp (+0.54 to +3.52 pp); Q3 +0.86 pp (-0.21 to +1.94 pp); Q4 +2.21 pp (+1.19 to +3.22 pp). By test-change ratio the highest rate is (0, 0.1] (32.49%, n=5,949) and the lowest 0 (source only) (28.21%, n=56,497). The 8-cell table: Pearson χ² = 296.5 (dof 7, n=128,617), p = 3.42e-60; effect size Cramér's V = 0.048 (negligible). Tests changed vs not: Within projects (Mantel-Haenszel over 361 projects with both groups, n=124,774): pooled odds ratio 1.10 (95% CI 1.07–1.14), CMH p = 7.59e-09; crude odds ratio on the same builds 1.17 (95% CI 1.14–1.20) (1.18 over all labelled builds, incl. projects with one group only); the association persists within projects but is weaker than the crude one.
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. Changing tests may go together with larger or riskier changes.
With n in the tens of thousands even negligible differences reach tiny p-values: read the effect size and its interval, not the p-value.
Ties: 32.19% of these builds have src_churn = 0, so the quartile groups are cut-point groups of unequal size, not equal quarters.

findings.title: Previous build outcome → next build outcome
findings.question: Does a failed previous build go with a failing next build?

population.description: labelled builds with a previous build that has an outcome

leakage_safe.definition: the project's build with an outcome whose finish is the latest one strictly before this build started (finish = started_at + duration, an upper bound): rl_core.features.history, feature prev_build_failed

within_projects.description: previous FINISHED build failed vs passed, stratified by project

naive.definition: the project's build that STARTED just before (started_at, build_id), finished or not: int_build_history.naive_prev_label

within_projects.description: previous STARTED build failed vs passed, stratified by project

findings.summary: Leakage-safe (previous FINISHED build, rl_core feature prev_build_failed): P(fail | previous failed) = 70.94% (70.47–71.40%, n=36,790) vs P(fail | previous passed) = 12.07% (11.86–12.29%, n=91,379), a difference of +58.86 pp (95% CI +58.35 to +59.37 pp). Naive (previous STARTED build): 72.28% (n=37,183) vs 11.25% (n=90,864), +61.03 pp (95% CI +60.53 to +61.52 pp), larger than the leakage-safe difference. For 28,090 of 128,047 naive pairs (21.94%) the naive predecessor is not known to have finished when the build started (its upper-bound finish, start + summed job time, is not before the build's start), so its outcome may not have existed at prediction time; on those overlapping pairs the difference is +67.67 pp vs +58.89 pp on pairs whose predecessor had finished. The two links give the same previous outcome for 122,245 of 128,001 builds (95.50%). Leakage-safe: Within projects (Mantel-Haenszel over 382 projects with both groups, n=123,014): pooled odds ratio 7.38 (95% CI 7.14–7.63), CMH p = < 1e-300; crude odds ratio on the same builds 14.56 (95% CI 14.12–15.01) (17.78 over all labelled builds, incl. projects with one group only); the association persists within projects but is weaker than the crude one.
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. Consecutive builds share the project, branch state, contributors and infrastructure, so a failure followed by a failure can reflect a broken state that persisted; the association does not show that one build's outcome affects the next.
Only the leakage-safe association is usable at prediction time (ADR-0006); the naive link uses, for overlapping builds, outcomes that may not yet have been known.
Finish times are upper bounds (started_at + summed job time), so the leakage-safe rule discards some builds that had in fact finished (conservative).

findings.title: CI duration: passed vs failed builds
findings.question: Do failed builds run longer or shorter than passed builds?

population.description: labelled builds with a duration (tr_duration = summed job time)

findings.summary: Median summed job time: failed 570 s (IQR 185 s–1,692 s, n=37,326) vs passed 420 s (IQR 205 s–1,104 s, n=91,282); median difference 150 s (95% bootstrap CI 134 s to 165.5 s). Mann-Whitney U = 1,836,777,278.5, p = 1.21e-107; Cliff's delta = 0.078 (negligible): P(failed longer) - P(passed longer). Failed builds are more spread out: a lower 25th and a higher 75th percentile than passed builds (consistent with some failures stopping early and others running longer).
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed.
Duration is Travis' tr_duration, the SUM of job times, not wall-clock: builds with more jobs (a larger matrix) are longer by construction.

Failures may stop early (fail-fast, a broken compile) or run until a time-out, and errored builds often break during setup; durations of failed builds mix these, so the difference need not say anything about the change itself.
Duration is a post-build observation: never a model input for the current build.

findings.title: Failure rate by project
findings.question: How much do failure rates differ between projects?

population.description: labelled builds of projects with ≥ 200 labelled builds

findings.summary: 161 of 402 projects have ≥ 200 labelled builds (105,512 of 128,617 builds). Their failure rates range from 1.82% to 100.00% (median 17.08%, IQR 9.96%–34.30%). Highest: apache/drill 100.00%, apache/sling 100.00%, deeplearning4j/deeplearning4j 86.49%. Lowest: tananaev/traccar 1.82%, iluwatar/java-design-patterns 2.40%, rhuss/docker-maven-plugin 2.58%. 2 of these projects never passed a build (apache/drill (n=419), apache/sling (n=3,797)); 0 never failed. Project vs failure: Pearson χ² = 30,623.1 (dof 160, n=105,512), p = < 1e-300; effect size Cramér's V = 0.539 (large).
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. Projects differ in size, language tooling, test suites, CI configuration and activity period.

A project that never passes more plausibly has a CI configuration that never worked (or a data artefact) than only risky changes; its builds add only failed → failed pairs, which inflates pooled (crude) associations such as previous-build → next-build.
A project's rate pools its whole observed history (2011-2015).

findings.title: Monthly reliability trend
findings.question: How does the failure rate move over calendar time?

population.description: labelled builds by UTC month of started_at

findings.summary: 50 months (2011-06 to 2015-08); 9 have fewer than 100 labelled builds and are flagged. Among the other 41, the monthly failure rate ranges from 12.37% (2012-11, n=380) to 34.59% (2012-07, n=318). Month vs failure: Pearson χ² = 702.4 (dof 40, n=128,482), p = 6.14e-122; effect size Cramér's V = 0.074 (negligible).
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. The mix of projects changes from month to month (see the projects column), so a monthly rate also reflects which projects were active, not calendar time alone.
Months with few builds have wide intervals; flagged months are kept in the series but excluded from the chi-square test.

findings.title: Core-team vs non-core contributors
findings.question: Do builds of core-team members' commits fail less often?

within_projects.description: core team vs non-core, stratified by project

findings.summary: core team: 27.55% (27.27–27.83%, n=100,690); non-core: 34.36% (33.80–34.92%, n=27,927). Difference -6.81 pp (95% CI -7.43 to -6.19 pp), risk ratio 0.80 (95% CI 0.79–0.82). Pearson χ² = 491.8 (dof 1, n=128,617), p = 5.79e-109; effect size Cramér's V = 0.062 (negligible). Within projects (Mantel-Haenszel over 337 projects with both groups, n=121,067): pooled odds ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.97–1.06), CMH p = 0.5366; crude odds ratio on the same builds 0.74 (95% CI 0.72–0.76) (0.73 over all labelled builds, incl. projects with one group only); the interval includes 1: no association is detectable within projects.
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. Core team = TravisTorrent's gh_by_core_team_member: the build's commit authors all belong to the developers who committed or merged pull requests in the 3 months before the build (docs/data/FEATURE_DEFINITIONS.md); experience, the kind of change and review all differ between the groups.
With n in the tens of thousands even negligible differences reach tiny p-values: read the effect size and its interval, not the p-value.

findings.title: Pull-request vs push builds
findings.question: Do pull-request builds fail more or less often than push builds?

within_projects.description: pull request vs push, stratified by project

findings.summary: pull request: 22.98% (22.38–23.60%, n=18,127); push: 30.02% (29.75–30.29%, n=110,490). Difference -7.04 pp (95% CI -7.70 to -6.36 pp), risk ratio 0.77 (95% CI 0.74–0.79). Pearson χ² = 374.4 (dof 1, n=128,617), p = 2.10e-83; effect size Cramér's V = 0.054 (negligible). Within projects (Mantel-Haenszel over 345 projects with both groups, n=107,589): pooled odds ratio 1.01 (95% CI 0.97–1.07), CMH p = 0.5436; crude odds ratio on the same builds 0.87 (95% CI 0.84–0.91) (0.70 over all labelled builds, incl. projects with one group only); the interval includes 1: no association is detectable within projects.
caveats: Association, not causation: observational data with no controlled assignment; project, period, author and change type are not held fixed. gh_is_pr: a PR build tests GitHub's merge of the PR into its base; 'push' is every non-PR build. The contributor mix differs between the two (series by_core_team).
With n in the tens of thousands even negligible differences reach tiny p-values: read the effect size and its interval, not the p-value.
